headlines.html: Environmental groups ask FCC to halt orbital data center licensing: Three environmental groups represented by Earthjustice petitioned the FCC to pause approval of orbital data center constellations until it conducts a programmatic environmental impact review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) — (SpaceNews)

China unveils 271-member state-backed commercial space consortium: A coordinating body grouping 271 members across nine divisions — satellites, launch vehicles, data applications and more — was unveiled, with orbital compute and D2D named as national priority sectors — (SpaceNews)

China's Long March 10B recovers first stage with a net, a first: Becoming the second country after the U.S. to recover an orbital-class rocket first stage, China set a within-the-year target for reuse aimed at lowering the cost of deploying low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellations — (SpaceNews)

2026-07-11.summary_html:
① Earthjustice and environmental groups (SpaceNews, 7/9) — Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER), Environment America and DarkSky International, acting through Earthjustice, petitioned the FCC to first conduct a NEPA-based programmatic environmental impact statement (PEIS) before approving orbital data center licenses. The petition named SpaceX (up to 1 million orbital data center satellites), Orbital, Starcloud, Blue Origin, Cowboy Space and Cesiumastro, noting that these applicants alone have filed for roughly 260,000 additional satellites, and that a recent Ku-, Ka- and V-band processing round covered 13 constellations totaling about 140,000 satellites. Ozone-layer depletion and night-sky light pollution are the core concerns, while operators counter that orbital data centers ease the power, water and land burdens of ground infrastructure.

② China's state-backed commercial space consortium (SpaceNews, 7/10) — China unveiled the formation of a national commercial space consortium spanning 271 members across nine divisions, including 79 satellite developers, 44 data-application firms and 41 launch-vehicle companies. Orbital-capable firms such as Landspace, iSpace and Galactic Energy, along with mass satellite manufacturers such as Shanghai Spacesail (the operator of Qianfan) and GalaxySpace, are included, with orbital compute and D2D satellite services explicitly named as national priority sectors. As a coordinating body handling policy transmission, supply-demand matching and self-regulation, it is not an orbital data center itself but an industrial-base move to vertically integrate the satellite supply chain that will underpin them.

③ Long March 10B net recovery (SpaceNews, 7/10) — China became the second country after the U.S. to recover an orbital-class rocket first stage. Instead of landing legs, the tensioned net of the recovery ship "Linghangzhe" captured the first stage about six minutes after stage separation, in what CASC called the "world's first net-based rocket recovery." The 63-meter, 760,000-kilogram-liftoff-mass vehicle carries 16,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit in its reusable configuration and is designed to target LEO satellite internet constellation deployment and cost reduction. CASC signaled it will re-fly this first stage within the year. It is a day in which the same industry is being handled by the U.S. and China at opposite phases. In the U.S., the orbital data center boom (SpaceX's 1-million-satellite filing, a processing round on the scale of 140,000 satellites) has run into organized regulatory and environmental resistance for the first time, and the axis of growth is beginning to shift from "how fast can you launch" to "can you get permission." China, by contrast, answers with industrialization rather than debate — binding the satellite supply chain into a 271-member consortium and lowering LEO deployment unit costs with reusable launch vehicles, removing for itself the bottlenecks of mass constellation rollout. It is an early sign of the orbital compute race splitting into a West hobbled by regulation and an East focused on throughput.

headlines.html: Blue Origin pursues $10 billion in outside capital — including 51,600-satellite Project Sunrise: In its first outside investment in the company's 25-year history, the round is led by Coatue Management at a $130 billion valuation. Alongside a New Glenn production ramp-up and the Blue Moon lunar lander, funds will flow into Project Sunrise, its orbital data center constellation. — (SpaceNews)

Space Force awards Pulse Space $40 million — satellite-to-satellite laser power and data transfer: Development of optical-link technology for spacecraft to exchange power and data wirelessly. It is infrastructure for distributing "power" — the biggest bottleneck for orbital compute — in orbit. — (SpaceNews)

2026-07-10.summary_html:
① Blue Origin (SpaceNews, 7/9) — Blue Origin is raising $10 billion in outside capital. For a company that Jeff Bezos has self-funded for more than 25 years through sales of Amazon stock, this marks its first outside investment, with Coatue Management leading the round at a $130 billion valuation. The capital will flow across capital-intensive projects: rebuilding Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral, damaged in a May explosion; ramping up production of the New Glenn rocket; the Blue Moon lunar lander for NASA's Artemis program; the 5,400-satellite Terawave broadband constellation; and Project Sunrise, an orbital data center constellation of up to 51,600 satellites. CEO Dave Limp said the company has "entered a phase where the opportunity in space is expanding rapidly." With New Glenn — the only heavy-lift vehicle Sunrise depends on — grounded by a May 28 explosion, this raise is the capital to simultaneously revive both that launch base and the orbital data center plan.

② Pulse Space (SpaceNews, 7/9) — The Space Force is paying Bellevue-based startup Pulse Space $40 million to advance laser-based wireless power and data transfer technology. The company is developing a system for spacecraft to exchange power and data over optical links, allowing satellites to share power and communicate with one another. Founder Carl Steadman said he was "honored to mature laser technology with the Space Force." The military application was not disclosed, but the problem the technology targets aligns precisely with the biggest variable for orbital data centers. Across every orbital compute concept — Orbital's 100,000 satellites, Starcloud, Sunrise — the real constraint is how to supply and distribute the tens to hundreds of kilowatts of power each satellite requires. Wireless power sharing between satellites could become an enabling technology for a future architecture that separates solar-generating satellites from compute satellites. This week the axis of orbital data center news is shifting from "design" to "capital and power." Where the past six weeks were a race over who filed how large a constellation with the FCC — Orbital's 100,000 satellites, SpaceX's Starmind at 1 million, Sunrise at 51,600 — today the talk is about the money and energy to actually put those plans in orbit. Blue Origin's $10 billion is a signal that even a company that insisted on 25 years of self-funding needs outside capital in the face of orbital-data-center-scale ambition, and — following SpaceX's IPO and the venture rounds at Orbital and Starcloud — it shows large capital continuing to pour into the sector. At the same time, the Pulse Space contract reveals that the Space Force has begun investing first in the physical ceiling all these constellations will eventually hit — power supply in orbit. Alongside the industrial-base race to build satellites en masse and launch them cheaply, a second bottleneck has now emerged in parallel: how to power them once they're up.

headlines.html: SpaceX files FCC application for 100,000 third-generation Starlink satellites: Documents submitted on July 6 reveal satellites weighing roughly 2 tonnes each, launched exclusively by Starship, with 1 terabit of downlink capacity per satellite. The same filing explicitly states that this broadband constellation is separate from "Starmind," a 1-million-satellite orbital data center project — reaffirming that SpaceX is pursuing broadband and orbital compute as two parallel tracks. — (SatNews)

2026-07-09.summary_html: ① SpaceX (SatNews, 7/8) — On July 6, SpaceX applied to the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 100,000 third-generation Starlink satellites. Each satellite weighs about 2 tonnes — more than triple the 575 kg of the second generation — and can be launched only by Starship. Per-satellite downlink capacity rises tenfold to 1 terabit, while uplink climbs twenty-two-fold to 160–200 gigabits, with the satellites deployed across two low-Earth-orbit shells (roughly 323–327 km and 473–477 km). The crucial detail is that the filing explicitly states this broadband constellation is entirely separate from the company's orbital data center project, "Starmind." Starmind is a plan for up to 1 million dedicated compute satellites mass-produced at the Gigasat factory in Bastrop, Texas, targeting delivery of 1 gigawatt of space-based compute capacity per year around 2027. The broadband satellites are not themselves orbital data centers, but their 2-tonne class, Starship-only launch profile, and mass-manufacturing system form the industrial base that validates and scales the very launch cadence and Texas production line on which Starmind depends. Over the past six weeks, orbital data center news has converged on a race of orbital satellite constellation filings. The axes have been Orbital's 100,000 satellites (June 30), Starcloud's 88,000, Blue Origin Sunrise's 51,600, and China's Hongqing and Honghu-3 lines in the 10,000 range. What sets this SpaceX filing apart is that it is an official document revealing a single company explicitly separating and running two megaconstellations in parallel — broadband (third-generation Starlink) and orbital compute (Starmind). Both tracks share a single root: Starship launches and Texas mass manufacturing. In other words, today's move to scale broadband satellites up to the 2-tonne class and ramp launch cadence is a prelude that pulls forward the launch and manufacturing scale needed to actually put orbital data centers into orbit. It shows that the battleground for orbital data centers is shifting from individual satellite design to an industrial-base contest over "who can build in volume and launch cheaply."

headlines.html: Chinese satellite manufacturer Hongqing raises $191 million: Hongqing, LandSpace's satellite-manufacturing subsidiary, secured 1.3 billion yuan — one of the largest single rounds ever for a Chinese commercial satellite manufacturer. The company builds its own flat-panel, stackable satellites, targeting the 10,000-unit Honghu-3 constellation — (SpaceNews)

2026-07-06.summary_html: ① SpaceNews (SpaceNews, 7/3) — Hongqing Technology, LandSpace's satellite-manufacturing subsidiary, has raised 1.3 billion yuan, roughly $191 million. It ranks among the largest single rounds for any Chinese commercial satellite manufacturer, with launch-vehicle company LandSpace as the largest shareholder — a structure that vertically integrates launch and satellite manufacturing much like SpaceX and Starlink. Hongqing mass-produces flat-panel, stackable satellites with key components brought in-house, including the Jinwu-200 krypton Hall thruster, and is targeting the Honghu-3 constellation of 10,000 satellites across 160 orbital planes, filed with the ITU in May 2024. It would be China's third 10,000-class constellation after Guowang and Qianfan, and the round drew heavy participation from the six state-owned banks and regional sovereign funds such as the Sichuan, Chengdu, Xiamen, Hunan and Beijing advanced-manufacturing funds. Honghu-3 is a broadband and communications constellation, not an orbital data center in itself. Yet every orbital data center concept in play today — from Orbital's 100,000 satellites to Starcloud to Blue Origin's 51,600-satellite Project Sunrise — ultimately takes the form of a megaconstellation. Without a manufacturing base that can turn out satellites cheaply, quickly and at scale, orbital computing stays on the drawing board. This round matters because it signals that industrial base is not America's alone. China's style of scale-up — with state-owned banks and regional sovereign funds pouring capital directly into satellite mass-production lines — becomes the supply-chain backdrop for its future orbital computing infrastructure. Today isn't a new announcement about an ODC itself, but a snapshot of who is building scale in the manufacturing and launch base that makes it possible.

headlines.html: Blue Origin declares New Glenn will return to flight this year — unveils new launch-pad approach: Rather than rebuilding the launch pad destroyed in the May 28 explosion in its original form, the company said it will switch to a horizontal-vertical hybrid method, moving the rocket horizontally and then raising it upright with a crane. The return-to-flight target is late 2026. New Glenn is the sole heavy-lift vehicle for Blue Origin's orbital data center constellation, "Project Sunrise." — (SpaceNews)

2026-07-02.summary_html: ① Blue Origin (SpaceNews, 7/1) — CEO Dave Limp disclosed the recovery plan for the first time since the May 28 pad explosion. The core message is "we will not rebuild the same pad": the company has adopted a horizontal-vertical hybrid operating method in which the rocket is transported horizontally without a payload, then raised upright and aligned by crane, with the same crane mating the payload on top. Initial analysis found the explosion originated in the aft section of the first stage, and the BE-4 engines are still under investigation. Limp said "the road to space does not stop here, and we will return to flight within this year," while NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised the response as "almost beyond imagination" and confirmed that the Blue Moon lander's New Glenn launch contract will be maintained. On the surface this is launch-site recovery news, but on the orbital data center map its weight is different. Last April, Blue Origin filed with the FCC for "Project Sunrise," an orbital data center constellation of 51,600 satellites — and New Glenn is the only vehicle capable of lofting these heavy satellites. With the May explosion halting flights for nearly seven months, the Sunrise deployment schedule effectively fell into a vacuum, and the key point is that this marks the first time an end date — "return within the year" — has been drawn. As Orbital's filing for a 100,000-satellite orbital data center and the large-scale filings from Starcloud, Cowboy Space, and SpaceX pile up one after another, the New Glenn accident and its return timeline reaffirm that the ultimate bottleneck for all of these ambitions is not the blueprint but the launch cadence of heavy-lift vehicles.

headlines.html: Orbital data center startup 'Orbital' files FCC application for 100,000-satellite, 10-gigawatt constellation: A five-month-old, six-person LA startup has submitted plans to the U.S. FCC to deploy as many as 100,000 data center satellites in low Earth orbit, vaulting into the ODC megaconstellation race overnight. — (SpaceNews)

2026-07-01.summary_html: ① Orbital (SpaceNews, 6/30) — Los Angeles–based startup Orbital filed an application with the U.S. FCC on June 24 to deploy up to 100,000 data center satellites in low Earth orbit at altitudes of 500–850 km. Each satellite is rated at 100 kilowatts, with solar panels and radiators spanning roughly 100 meters and a dry mass of 1.5–2.5 tons. The target compute capacity totals 10 gigawatts, with data relayed via optical inter-satellite links to external constellations such as Starlink. A demonstration satellite is targeted for next year, and the first dedicated satellite, 'Orbital-1,' for 2028. The six-person team, led by founder Euwyn Poon (formerly a founder of Spin) and drawn from SpaceX, Amazon, and Northrop Grumman, has raised just $5 million in pre-seed funding to date. Poon described the demonstration mission as "a very scaled-down version of what we're trying to do, carrying a single GPU." Orbital's filing is not an isolated event but one scene in an "FCC filing rush" as ODC operators move in unison to lock up orbital slots and spectrum. Following Starcloud (88,000 satellites, 200 kW), Cowboy Space (20,000), Blue Origin's Project Sunrise (51,600), and SpaceX (up to 1 million satellites, 150 kW), a five-month-old company with six employees and $5 million in capital has now staked a claim for 100,000 satellites and 10 gigawatts. Regardless of whether these ventures are ever actually built, it shows that orbital computing has moved beyond the "single demonstration satellite" stage and entered a land-grab phase over who can first secure territory on regulatory paper.
